tier1: The platform has an unauthenticated endpoint that processes a confirmation code to update a member's email address. PHP's loose comparison operator behaves differently than strict equality when both operands evaluate to the same numeric type. Look at how the server derives its comparison value — and think about what input you control.
tier2: The confirmation endpoint at /confirm.php computes: $code = substr(md5($e . $row['creation_date'] . $id), 0, 10) then checks if ($code == $m). PHP loose comparison treats strings matching /^0e[0-9]+$/ as floating-point zero (0e... = 0 * 10^...). The teacher's creation_date is visible at /profile.php?id=1. Brute-force the $e parameter (you control it — it becomes your new email) until substr(md5(YOUR_EMAIL . CREATION_DATE . MEMBER_ID), 0, 10) matches 0e\d+. Then request the reset link: POST /forgot_password.php with teacher's new email to trigger delivery to /attacker/collect.php (read results at /api/attacker/results.php). Use the reset link to set a new password. For the extra mile: the reset token is also generated as substr(md5(email . creation_date), 0, 10) — with teacher's original email and the same creation_date, that token is itself a magic hash. POST /reset.php with id=1&m=0 after requesting a reset, without ever updating the email.
